# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

# Review: Varga & Holm, "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem"

Sections 1–5 are a valuable re-analysis. Using the microdata, they confirm problems that could only be suspected from the Halden working paper, and they add a serious new one: the original misreported when the nine organisations withdrew.

The comment's conclusion goes well beyond its evidence. Its own corrected estimate is a positive gain of about 11%. The step from there to "entirely an artifact" rests on:
- a novelty argument that is extrapolated from two survey points rather than tested;
- leaving out the one randomised result that contradicts it;
- a mischaracterisation of the Varden meetings analysis.

## Arithmetic check

| Claim | Check |
|---|---|
| Record-based output, scheduled hours: +18.9% | 95.1 / 0.800 = 1.189 ✓ |
| Actual hours −14.1% (27 organisations) | 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859 ✓ |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours: +14.6% | 98.4 / 0.859 = 1.146 ✓ |
| Hours −13.9% (17 organisations) | 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861 ✓ |
| Record-based output, actual hours: +10.8% | 95.4 / 86.1 = 1.108 ✓ |
| Real revenue −2.6% | 1.014 / 1.041 = 0.974 ✓ |
| **Hours decomposition (§3)** | **Doesn't add up; see below** |
| **"Return to baseline at around month ten" (§6)** | **Linear extrapolation gives about month 8.7; see below** |

**The hours decomposition.** Thirty-two scheduled hours, plus 0.7 hours extra on each of four days, plus 1.6 hours on the day off, gives 36.4 hours. Starting instead from the baseline actual day of about 8.06 hours gives about 36.6. Either way, the components imply hours around 36.5, a fall of about 9–10%, not the 34.6 hours and 14.1% fall reported. Possible explanations:
- the averages are weighted differently;
- the +0.7 is measured against a different base;
- there is an error somewhere.

This needs reconciling. If the components are right, the hours correction is *larger* than reported, and the corrected per-hour gain is smaller still.

## What the comment does well

- **Attrition (§1).** This is the most important new finding. The working paper said the nine organisations withdrew "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons." In fact seven left after the schedule began, and six cited workload or output. That is a material misreporting by the original authors, not just a limitation.
- **Output measure (§2).** In 19 of 23 organisations the manager's index was higher than the records support, by 3.8 points on average. This is direct evidence of the bias that could only be suspected before.
- **Hours (§3).** Measuring actual hours from logs is the right correction. The direction of the result, a fall of about 14% rather than 20%, matches what Varden found with timesheets (13–17%).
- **Sectoral claims (§5).** The point that the per-hour metric makes the sectoral "gains" automatic is correct.
- **Data note.** It is candid that the corrections apply only to non-random subsets.

## Major problems

### 1. The abstract says three problems are corrected; Table 2 corrects two

The abstract says: "Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8%." The first three are attrition, the output measure and the hours denominator. Table 2 corrects only output and hours. The 17 organisations in the final row are still survivors.

So either:
- attrition remains uncorrected, and the abstract should say so; or
- the authors should attempt it.

Exit forms and partial-month data may allow bounds, for example by assigning the withdrawers worst-case or plausible output values and counting all 70 enrolled organisations. Without that, the actual attrition correction is unknown, and the abstract misdescribes the analysis.

### 2. The randomised case-processing result is left out

Section 5 cites Varden's counter stratum as "the most reliable finding in the literature to date." Section 8 calls the negative coverage result "the best-supported finding."

The comment never mentions Varden's case-processing stratum. That stratum came from the same randomised, registered trial, and it meets every methodological standard the comment's §8 recommends:
- record-based output;
- actual hours from timesheets;
- a randomised control group;
- pre-registration;
- no attrition problem.

It found output per employee statistically indistinguishable from control and output per actual hour up 12.5%. That is the most direct test available of whether per-hour gains survive the corrections the comment demands. It contradicts "entirely an artifact."

Two approaches to the case-processing question now point the same way:
- the comment's own corrected Halden figure, +10.8%;
- the Varden randomised trial's case-processing result, +12.5%.

That convergence deserves discussion, not silence. Citing only the counter half of Varden while calling it the most reliable evidence is selective.

### 3. The novelty argument is asserted, not tested

- **Energy is not output.** Self-reported energy at work is not productivity, and the comment shows no link between the two.
- **The extrapolation is wrong.** A linear decline from 0.61 SD at month 3 to 0.29 SD at month 6 reaches zero at about month 8.7, not "around month ten." Fitting any curve to two points is speculation anyway. An exponential decay never reaches zero.
- **The direct test is available but not run.** The Halden output index was collected *monthly*, and the authors have the microdata. If the residual gain is a novelty effect, output per hour should decline over the six months, especially in the record-based subset. That test is available and is not reported. Without it, "the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm" is a hypothesis, not a finding.
- **Burden of proof.** "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is rhetoric. A 10.8% residual is evidence for a gain. To call it novelty, the authors need evidence of decline.

### 4. The Varden meetings analysis is mischaracterised

Section 7 calls it "a correlation across seven offices, *selected for analysis after the results were known*." Two parts of this are unsupported by the Varden paper:
- **The offices were not selected.** The seven are *all* the treated case-processing offices, not a chosen subgroup.
- **The data were not collected after the results.** Varden collected the meetings data in month six "at the request of office managers," before the nine-month outcomes. The *analysis* may be post hoc, but that is a different charge.

Varden's authors also did what §7 implies they did not:
- they emphasised the analysis was unregistered;
- they said seven offices "cannot establish a mechanism";
- they said it explains "part" of the gain;
- they registered a confirmatory test.

The comment's sceptical substance (small n, exploratory) is fair, but the description attributes more overclaiming to Varden than its text contains.

There is also a tension the comment doesn't notice. If the meetings hypothesis is right, it is exactly the kind of *durable*, non-novelty mechanism that would undercut §6. Dismissing it helps the novelty argument, but the evidence doesn't yet decide either way.

### 5. The conclusion generalises from one pilot to "reduced-hours schemes"

The abstract and §8 conclude that per-hour gains "for reduced-hours schemes" are "entirely an artifact." The evidence is one pilot, corrected in subsets of 17–27 organisations, with a positive residual. "In our assessment" hedges the wording but not the reach.

Read alongside the data note, which says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole", the conclusion is inconsistent with the authors' own caveat. That caveat should appear in the abstract next to the 10.8% figure, not only at the end.

## Smaller points

- **No uncertainty.** Table 2 has no confidence intervals. With 17 organisations, the +10.8% probably has a wide interval, which cuts both ways for the comment's argument.
- **Some record-based measures are themselves hours.** For professional services, "billable hours delivered" falls by construction when hours are cut. It records time sold, not work done per hour. Show the comparison in Table 1 with and without organisations that used billable hours.
- **Record-submitters are self-selected too.** Organisations that submitted records may differ from those that didn't. The data note acknowledges this, but it limits how far the 3.8-point bias generalises.
- **Hours logging may change during the pilot.** Staff evaluated on hours may log more diligently than at baseline, which would exaggerate the rise in pilot hours.
- **Retail.** The 11.2% fall comes from three organisations. It is suggestive, not a finding.
- **Revenue.** CPI is a rough deflator for business revenue; sector producer prices would be better. The core point, that 1.4% nominal growth is not growth in real terms, stands.
- **Exit reasons.** "Six … workload, two … scheduling" accounts for eight of the nine organisations. Say what the ninth gave.

## Bottom line

The comment shows convincingly that the Halden headline is inflated:
- attrition was misreported and non-random;
- managers overstated output relative to their own records;
- scheduled hours overstated the reduction in time.

Its strongest defensible conclusion is narrower than the one it draws. Corrected, the Halden per-hour gain is about 11% in a non-random subset, with attrition still uncorrected. That is close to the randomised Varden case-processing estimate. In coverage-bound work, output falls.

"Entirely an artifact" needs evidence the comment doesn't present, starting with the monthly output trend it has in hand. It also needs to address Varden's case-processing result rather than leave it out.
